title: The Price of Convenience
text:
Every day, millions of people exchange small pieces of their private lives for convenience. A map application learns where its user lives and works; an online shop remembers what he buys and suggests what he might want next; a fitness band records his sleep and heartbeat. Each exchange seems trivial, and most people accept the terms without reading them. Yet taken together, these fragments form a detailed portrait of a person’s habits, health, relationships and beliefs.

The companies that collect such data argue that it allows them to offer free services and more relevant advertising. There is some truth in this; few users would wish to pay for every search or message they send. But the arrangement is less equal than it appears. Users rarely know how long their information is kept, with whom it is shared, or what conclusions are drawn from it. A person may be refused a loan or shown higher prices because of a profile he has never seen and cannot correct.

Privacy is sometimes dismissed with the remark that only those with something to hide need worry. This misunderstands its purpose. Privacy protects the freedom to think, to experiment and to make mistakes without being permanently recorded. It also guards against the misuse of information by whoever may control it in the future.

Protecting privacy does not require abandoning digital services. It requires clear rules on what may be collected, honest explanations in plain language, and a genuine right for individuals to see and delete what is held about them.

title: Learning to Live with Water
text:
For generations, the standard response to floods was to build walls against them. Embankments were raised along rivers, and each new flood prompted calls to make them higher and stronger. Such defences have saved many lives, but they carry a hidden risk. By creating a sense of complete safety, they encourage settlement on low-lying land, so that when an exceptional flood does overtop or break the wall, the damage is far greater than it would otherwise have been.

As a warming climate brings heavier rainfall and more intense storms to many regions, planners increasingly speak of adaptation rather than defence alone. The aim is not to keep every drop of water out but to reduce the harm it causes. In practice this can mean leaving certain fields free to flood so that rivers have room to spread, building schools and clinics on raised platforms, and restoring wetlands that soak up excess water like a sponge.

Early warning is equally important. A village that receives a reliable alert a day in advance can move people, livestock and grain to higher ground. Such systems depend less on expensive machinery than on trust: residents must believe the warnings and know exactly where to go.

Adaptation is not a substitute for reducing the emissions that drive climate change; the two must go together. But even if emissions fell sharply tomorrow, the changes already under way would continue for decades. Communities that learn to live with water, rather than simply fight it, will be better placed to endure the floods that are certain to come.

title: The Water We Eat
text:
When people think about saving water, they usually picture a dripping tap or a long shower. These matter, but they are a small part of the story. Far more water is used, out of sight, to grow the food we eat and to make the goods we buy. A loaf of bread, a cotton shirt or a bowl of rice carries within it the water that was needed to produce it, water that economists call “virtual” because it is no longer visibly present in the finished product.

The idea has important consequences for countries short of water. When a dry country grows thirsty crops for export, it is in effect sending its scarce water abroad in another form. Conversely, a country that imports grain is saving the water it would have needed to grow that grain itself. Some analysts argue that, for arid regions, importing water-intensive food and using local water for higher-value purposes may be wiser than striving for self-sufficiency in every crop.

The argument is not simple. Relying on imports exposes a country to sudden price rises and to decisions taken by foreign governments, and many farming families depend on the very crops that use the most water. An abrupt change in policy could cost them their livelihoods.

Nevertheless, the concept of virtual water encourages a more honest accounting. It reminds governments that decisions about agriculture and trade are also decisions about water, and that a country’s rivers and aquifers can be drained as surely through its exports as through its taps.

title: Why Rights Are Called Universal
text:
To call a right universal is to claim that it belongs to every human being simply by virtue of being human. It does not depend on nationality, wealth, religion, gender or the favour of a ruler. A prisoner, a refugee and a head of state possess the same basic entitlements: not to be tortured, not to be enslaved, and to be treated equally before the law.

This claim is more radical than it may appear. Throughout much of history, protections were privileges granted to particular groups, such as the citizens of a city, the members of a class or the followers of a faith. Outsiders could be treated very differently. The modern language of human rights insists that no such boundary can justify denying anyone the core of human dignity.

Critics sometimes object that universal rights are merely the values of one culture imposed on others. The objection deserves a serious answer. Many societies express respect for human dignity through their own moral and religious traditions, and the idea that the weak must be protected from the strong is hardly the property of any single civilisation. Universality does not require every country to organise its institutions identically; it requires that certain minimum protections apply everywhere.

The greatest difficulty lies not in stating rights but in securing them. A right written in a charter means little to a person who cannot reach a court, afford a lawyer or speak without fear. For this reason, the practical test of a society’s commitment to rights is how it treats those with the least power to insist on them.

subject: English
q: The passage mainly argues that:
o: the trade of personal data for convenience needs clearer rules and fairer terms
digital services should be abandoned in order to protect privacy
only people with something to hide need to worry about privacy
companies should stop offering free services
explanation: The author describes the unequal exchange of data for convenience and ends by calling for clear rules, honest explanations and a right to see and delete data.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, companies justify collecting data on the grounds that it:
o: allows free services and more relevant advertising
is required by governments
protects users from fraud
improves users’ health and sleep
explanation: The second paragraph says companies argue that data allows them to offer free services and more relevant advertising.

subject: English
q: The passage describes the arrangement between users and companies as unequal because users:
o: pay more for digital services than companies do
are required to buy fitness bands
seldom know how their information is kept, shared or used
cannot use map applications without paying
explanation: Users rarely know how long their information is kept, with whom it is shared, or what conclusions are drawn from it.

subject: English
q: The word ‘trivial’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: highly dangerous
very complicated
legally compulsory
of little importance
explanation: Each exchange “seems trivial”, yet together they form a detailed portrait; the contrast shows trivial means of little importance.

subject: English
q: It can be inferred that the author regards a profile that a person ‘has never seen and cannot correct’ as:
o: unfair, because it can affect decisions about him without his knowledge
harmless, because it is used only for advertising
reliable, because it is based on real data
unimportant, because few people are refused loans
explanation: The author offers the example of being refused a loan or shown higher prices to show how unequal and unfair the arrangement is.

subject: English
q: The third paragraph mainly serves to:
o: explain how companies build data profiles
describe the benefits of targeted advertising
list the rules needed to protect personal data
rebut a common argument that privacy matters only to wrongdoers
explanation: The paragraph quotes the remark that only those with something to hide need worry and argues that it misunderstands the purpose of privacy.

subject: English
q: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
o: Embankments should be abolished because they never save lives
Reducing emissions will stop floods within a few years
Communities must adapt to floods rather than rely only on walls against them
Early warning systems depend mainly on costly machinery
explanation: The passage argues for adaptation, reducing the harm water causes, alongside or beyond the traditional defence of building walls.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, restored wetlands help by:
o: soaking up excess water like a sponge
raising the height of embankments
sending early warnings to villages
providing land for new settlements
explanation: The second paragraph mentions restoring wetlands that soak up excess water like a sponge.

subject: English
q: The passage says that the success of early warning systems depends mainly on:
o: residents trusting the warnings and knowing where to go
the purchase of expensive machinery
the height of nearby river embankments
the number of schools built on platforms
explanation: The third paragraph says such systems depend less on expensive machinery than on trust: residents must believe the warnings and know where to go.

subject: English
q: The ‘hidden risk’ of embankments, as described in the passage, is that they:
o: cost more to build than the damage floods cause
make rivers flow faster and dry up nearby fields
encourage people to settle where an exceptional flood would do great harm
prevent governments from issuing flood warnings
explanation: By creating a sense of complete safety, embankments encourage settlement on low-lying land, so a flood that breaks through does far greater damage.

subject: English
q: The word ‘endure’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: prevent
withstand
predict
welcome
explanation: Communities that adapt will be better placed to endure floods that are certain to come, that is, to withstand them, since they cannot be prevented.

subject: English
q: The author’s approach to the problem of floods can best be described as:
o: resigned and fatalistic
scornful and dismissive
sentimental and nostalgic
practical and forward-looking
explanation: The author accepts that floods will come but proposes concrete measures such as room for rivers, raised buildings and early warning.

subject: English
q: The passage is chiefly concerned with:
o: the water hidden in the production of food and goods
methods of repairing dripping taps
the history of the grain trade between nations
the causes of drought in arid regions
explanation: The passage introduces “virtual” water, the water used out of sight to produce food and goods, and discusses its consequences.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, why is the water used to make products called ‘virtual’?
o: It is imaginary and has no real cost
It is no longer visibly present in the finished product
It can be measured only by computers
It comes from underground aquifers
explanation: The first paragraph says economists call it virtual because it is no longer visibly present in the finished product.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, a dry country that exports thirsty crops is:
o: saving water it would otherwise need
protecting its farmers from price rises
in effect sending its scarce water abroad
achieving self-sufficiency in every crop
explanation: The second paragraph states that such a country is in effect sending its scarce water abroad in another form.

subject: English
q: The word ‘arid’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: densely populated
highly fertile
mountainous
very dry
explanation: Arid regions are those short of water, which is why importing water-intensive food is suggested for them.

subject: English
q: The third paragraph indicates that the author regards the case for importing water-intensive food as:
o: entirely mistaken
free of any drawbacks
relevant only to wealthy nations
reasonable but carrying real risks
explanation: The author says “the argument is not simple”, pointing to price rises, foreign decisions and farmers’ livelihoods, yet still defends the concept in the final paragraph.

subject: English
q: The author’s purpose in the final paragraph is to:
o: urge countries to stop all agricultural exports
stress that trade and farming policies are also water policies
explain how underground aquifers are formed
defend the goal of complete self-sufficiency
explanation: The last paragraph says decisions about agriculture and trade are also decisions about water.

subject: English
q: The passage is mainly about:
o: the history of one particular international charter
why rights should depend on citizenship
the meaning of universal rights and the difficulty of securing them
how courts are organised in different countries
explanation: The passage defines universal rights, answers the charge of cultural bias, and ends by noting that securing rights is harder than stating them.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, a universal right belongs to a person because he or she:
o: is a citizen of a state
is a human being
follows a particular faith
has been granted it by a ruler
explanation: The first sentence says a universal right belongs to every human being simply by virtue of being human.

subject: English
q: How does the passage describe protections throughout much of history?
o: As privileges granted to particular groups
As rights shared equally by all people
As rules imposed by foreign powers
As customs that applied only to rulers
explanation: The second paragraph says protections were privileges granted to particular groups such as citizens, a class or followers of a faith.

subject: English
q: The word ‘radical’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: far-reaching and fundamental
politically violent
widely accepted
carefully limited
explanation: The claim is radical because it overturns the historical pattern of protections for particular groups only; it is fundamental, not violent.

subject: English
q: In replying to critics, the author suggests that universality:
o: requires common minimum protections, not identical institutions
means every country must adopt the same laws
reflects the values of a single culture
cannot be defended against criticism
explanation: The author says universality does not require identical institutions; it requires that certain minimum protections apply everywhere.

subject: English
q: The author mentions a prisoner, a refugee and a head of state together in order to show that:
o: prisoners should be treated as heads of state
refugees have more rights than citizens
rulers are free from the law
people of very different status hold the same basic rights
explanation: The three figures, far apart in status, are said to possess the same basic entitlements, which illustrates universality.
